title: Wild Bushbean: How to Spot and Control It in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Wild Bushbean in Rice Fields: Identify and Control It
metaDescription: Wild bushbean, or Balabalatong, is a bean family weed of rainfed palay. Learn to spot its red purple flowers and long pods and stop it early.
excerpt: Wild bushbean is an upright, bean family weed that farmers call Balabalatong. It shows up in rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines, where the soil is not always flooded. This page shows you how to spot it by its three part leaves and long pods, and how to control it before the pods ripen.

heroImage.alt: Wild bushbean (Macroptilium lathyroides), a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: DouglasGoldman, CC BY SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
Wild bushbean belongs to the bean family, Papilionaceae, also called Leguminosae. Its scientific name is Macroptilium lathyroides, and farmers know it as Balabalatong. Since it is a broadleaf weed, it is not a grass or a sedge. Like other legumes, it carries its seeds in long pods, much like the beans you grow at home.

You will find it in rainfed lowland rice fields. As an annual, each plant lives for one season and then dies. Seed is its only way to spread. The long pods turn from green to brown as they ripen, and the seeds inside fall to the ground. Then those seeds wait in the soil and sprout when the next rains come.

Look for an upright plant with branched stems that feel woody. Each leaf is made of three leaflets, like a bean leaf, and the leaflets are oval to lance shaped. As a broadleaf weed, it has wide leaves with netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. The flowers are red purple. After flowering, it forms long, slender pods that start green and turn brown when mature.

items: Upright plants with branched stems that feel woody when you bend them.
Leaves made of three leaflets, each oval to lance shaped, like a bean leaf.
Red purple flowers shaped like the flowers of other beans and peas.
Long, slender pods, green when young and brown when mature.
Leaves with netted veins, unlike the parallel veins of grassy weeds and sedges nearby.

blocks.text:
Wild bushbean competes with your palay for water, light and space. Its woody, branched stems spread out and shade nearby rice hills. Because it is a legume, it can make some of its own nitrogen, so it can still grow well where the soil is poor. It also takes water and other nutrients from the same root zone as the rice.

The bigger risk is the seed. Each plant fills many long pods, and the seeds drop into the field. Seeds caught at harvest can also mix with the palay and end up in seed you save. Weeds like this give pests a place to hide between the rice hills too. So one season of neglect can leave you with more weeding in the seasons that follow.

items: Pull the plants before the pods turn brown, because mature pods split open and drop their seeds onto the field.
Hand weed while the stems are still soft, since older plants with woody stems are hard to pull out with their roots.
Carry pulled plants with pods out of the paddy and dry them away from the field, instead of leaving them on the bund.
Where your water supply allows, keep standing water in the paddy early on, since its seeds sprout best on moist, unflooded soil.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold wild bushbean down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Wild Bushbean Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Wild Bushbean?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. You can also put the weeding days on your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar), so the team knows when to go in.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Wild Bushbean

items.q: What is wild bushbean called in Tagalog?
items.a: Farmers call it Balabalatong. Its scientific name is Macroptilium lathyroides. Local names can change from one province to the next, so do not rely on the name alone. Check for the three part leaves, the red purple flowers, and the long, slender pods that turn brown when they ripen.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Begin with a well prepared, level field and clean seed. Keep water in the paddy where you can. Hand weed early, while the stems are soft, and always before the pods turn brown. If you need a herbicide, choose one for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice, and follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does this weed keep coming back every season?
items.a: It is an annual, but it leaves plenty of seed behind. The long pods ripen, split open, and drop seeds into the soil. Those seeds sprout when the field gets wet again. If even a few plants set pods, the next cropping starts with a fresh flush of weeds. That is why pulling plants before the pods turn brown matters most.
